ai.definition: Mind uploading, also known as whole brain emulation or mind transfer, is a theoretical process aimed at transferring an individual's complete mental content from their biological brain to a computer system. This would allow the person’s consciousness and memories to exist within a virtual environment.
ai.howItWorks: The process involves creating detailed models of the human brain at the cellular level through advanced neuroimaging techniques, followed by precise mapping of neural connections and patterns. These models are then simulated in software or hardware environments capable of replicating brain functions. Neural interfaces would be developed to read and write directly from/to the brain’s neurons.
ai.problemSolved: Addresses issues related to longevity, immortality, and potential for enhanced cognitive abilities by allowing minds to exist beyond biological constraints.
ai.manufacturing: Highly speculative; requires breakthroughs in nanotechnology, neuroimaging, AI, and computational power. Current technology is not sufficient for precise brain emulation.
ai.buildProcess: Involves creating detailed maps of the human brain, developing sophisticated algorithms to simulate neural activity, and integrating these with advanced computing hardware capable of handling vast amounts of data.
ai.costDrivers: High due to the complexity and scale required. Cost drivers include R&D expenses for neuroimaging technologies, computational resources needed for simulations, and ethical considerations surrounding human subjects in experiments.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Long-term potential with significant barriers to entry. Current research is at a very early stage and faces numerous technical and ethical challenges.
ai.regulation: Currently unregulated; would require new frameworks addressing privacy, consent, and legal status of digital consciousness.
ai.risks: Includes safety risks from invasive procedures, ethical concerns about creating artificial consciousness, and potential for misuse or abuse of technology.
ai.profitability: Uncertain due to speculative nature. Potential long-term benefits could lead to significant economic impact but are currently unquantifiable.
ai.futureDevelopment: Depends on advancements in neuroscience, AI, and computing technologies. Collaboration between neuroscientists, engineers, ethicists, and policymakers will be crucial.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units would draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking and other precision manufacturing processes.

glossary.def: A device that can read from or write to the nervous system, enabling communication between biological and artificial systems.
The process of creating a functional model of an entire brain in software, capable of simulating its cognitive functions.
Techniques used to visualize the structure and function of the nervous system, including MRI, CT scans, and fMRI.

subsystems.name: Specimen preparation
subsystems.role: gets a brain into a state where every synapse can be imaged.

subsystems.name: Volumetric imaging
subsystems.role: captures the tissue at nanometre resolution.

subsystems.name: Image processing pipeline
subsystems.role: turns petabytes of images into labelled cells and connections.

subsystems.name: Connectome and state model
subsystems.role: stores the wiring diagram plus what each synapse does.

subsystems.name: Emulation substrate
subsystems.role: runs the reconstructed network fast enough to behave in real time.
parts: large GPU or specialised compute cluster

subsystems.name: Simulation software
subsystems.role: models neurons and synapses and lets the network interact with a virtual body and senses.

buildSteps.title: Obtain and preserve a brain
buildSteps.detail: A whole human brain must be fixed quickly after death and stabilised so that fine structure survives years of imaging. Note that the quantum-entanglement method sometimes described has no scientific basis; real work is physical imaging.

buildSteps.title: Cut and image the tissue
buildSteps.detail: The brain is sliced into tens of thousands of thin sections, or scanned block-face, and each is imaged by electron microscopy until every synaptic contact is resolvable. Imaging one cubic millimetre of tissue already takes months.

buildSteps.title: Align and segment
buildSteps.detail: Software stitches the images into a 3D volume, then machine-learning models trace every neuron and find every synapse, with human proofreaders correcting errors.

buildSteps.title: Infer function, not just wiring
buildSteps.detail: Wiring alone is not a mind: the reconstruction must estimate which synapses excite or inhibit, their strength, and the internal state of each cell.

buildSteps.title: Build the simulation
buildSteps.detail: Each reconstructed neuron becomes a mathematical model on a computer, wired up as in the connectome.

buildSteps.title: Validate against behaviour
buildSteps.detail: Small networks — retina, insect circuits — are simulated and their output compared with real recordings until they match.

buildSteps.title: Close the loop
buildSteps.detail: The simulated brain is connected to simulated senses and a body, and its behaviour is tested. Only then would anyone claim a mind had been copied.

prerequisites.why: complete wiring diagrams now exist for the nematode worm (1986) and the fruit fly (2020s), and for small human cortex samples, but not for a whole human brain.
current synapse-resolution imaging destroys the tissue; uploading a living person would need a method that does not.
memory and personality are thought to live partly in synapse strengths and molecular states, which cannot yet be read out at whole-brain scale.
simulating tens of billions of neurons with detailed synapses needs far more compute than is available today.

prerequisites.tech: A validated theory of neural coding
prerequisites.why: without knowing how networks encode information, an accurate copy could not be checked.

pathway.milestone: complete connectomes of small animals and millimetre-scale human cortex samples
pathway.unlocks: methods for automated segmentation and proofreading at scale.

pathway.milestone: whole mouse brain connectome plus functional maps
pathway.unlocks: testing whether wiring diagrams alone predict behaviour.

pathway.milestone: non-destructive, living-brain scanning at synapse resolution
pathway.unlocks: theoretical route to copying a mind without destroying it, if it is physically possible at all.

pathway.milestone: whole human brain emulation running in real time
pathway.unlocks: the claimed goal — and hard questions about whether the copy is the same person, which no engineering step can settle.
